Then he alluded to consoling him, peace and blessings be upon him, regarding their mockery, within a threat to them, by His saying, exalted is He:

The discussion of His saying, Exalted is He:

[41] ﴿And messengers before you were certainly mocked, but those who mocked them were enveloped by that which they used to mock.﴾

﴿And messengers before you were certainly mocked, but [those who mocked were] enveloped﴾, i.e., descended upon: ﴿those who mocked them were enveloped by that which they used to mock﴾, i.e., its punishment or its recompense, by placing the cause in the place of the effect, to signal the complete connection between the two; or it is the very mockery itself, if by this is meant the punishment of the Hereafter, based on the embodiment of deeds (tajassum al-a'mal). For the outward deeds in this created existence take on an accidental form, and they appear in the next existence in essential forms, suited to them in goodness and ugliness. This is related from Abu al-Su'ud.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 21, verses 42–43:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[42] ﴿Say: "Who can protect you by night and by day from the Most Merciful?" Yet they turn away from the remembrance of their Lord.﴾ [43] ﴿Or do they have gods who can defend them against Us? They are unable even to help themselves, nor will they be accompanied (protected) from Us.﴾ [al-Anbiya: 43].

﴿Say: "Who can protect you﴾ — i.e., who can guard you — ﴿by night and by day from the Most Merciful﴾, i.e., from His punishment, i.e., when it comes upon you suddenly. The mention of "night" first is because calamities occur more frequently at night and their impact is more severe. The word "the Most Merciful" (al-Rahman) is a reminder that there is no protection for them except through His mercy, and it provides them with the answer. It has also been said that it is an indication of His severity, like the anger of the forbearing one, and a rebuke to them, in that He punishes them, though His mercy prevails. And it indicates the extreme wickedness of them. Al-Mahayimi said: "His general mercy does not preclude this, for by punishing you, the people of your age and those after them are admonished, so that their affairs are set right, which calls for His mercy upon them; and they should not be deceived by the generality of His mercy into expecting that it will withhold this." ﴿Yet they turn away from the remembrance of their Lord﴾, i.e., they do not even bring Him to mind, let alone fear His punishment, and they do not count the security and ease they enjoy as a protection and safeguarding, so that they might be asked about the one who guards: ﴿Or do they have gods who can defend them against Us? They are unable even to help themselves, nor will they be accompanied (protected) from Us.﴾ [al-Anbiya: 43], i.e., for these who hasten their Lord's punishment, are there gods who can prevent them, if We bring down Our punishment upon them and send Our might upon them, from Us? Its meaning: Do they have gods other than Us who can prevent them from Us? Then the Exalted, whose praise is great, described those gods with weakness and humiliation and with what they are in terms of their attributes. Its meaning: how can their gods, whom they invoke other than Us, prevent them from Us, when they cannot help themselves and are not accompanied by Us with help and support? Ibn Jarir conveyed this.

So ﴿fa-yusbahuna﴾ (﴿yuṣḥabūna﴾) here carries the meaning of "to be given protection" (yujarun). It is said: "May God accompany you" (ṣahibaka Allah), i.e., may He grant you protection and keep you safe, as in al-Asas (Asas al-Balagha). Ibn Jarir said: i.e., they will not be accompanied by protection, because the Arabs have a reported usage: "I am your protector (jar) from so-and-so and your companion (sahib)," meaning: "I grant you protection and defend you." If they are not accompanied by protection, there will be no one to prevent them from the punishment of God, given His wrath upon them, so they will not be accompanied with good and will not be helped.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 21, verses 42–43:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[42] ﴿Say: "Who can protect you by night and by day from the Most Merciful?" Yet they turn away from the remembrance of their Lord.﴾ [43] ﴿Or do they have gods who can defend them against Us? They are unable even to help themselves, nor will they be accompanied (protected) from Us.﴾ [al-Anbiya: 43].

﴿Say: "Who can protect you﴾ — i.e., who can guard you — ﴿by night and by day from the Most Merciful﴾, i.e., from His punishment, i.e., when it comes upon you suddenly. The mention of "night" first is because calamities occur more frequently at night and their impact is more severe. The word "the Most Merciful" (al-Rahman) is a reminder that there is no protection for them except through His mercy, and it provides them with the answer. It has also been said that it is an indication of His severity, like the anger of the forbearing one, and a rebuke to them, in that He punishes them, though His mercy prevails. And it indicates the extreme wickedness of them. Al-Mahayimi said: "His general mercy does not preclude this, for by punishing you, the people of your age and those after them are admonished, so that their affairs are set right, which calls for His mercy upon them; and they should not be deceived by the generality of His mercy into expecting that it will withhold this." ﴿Yet they turn away from the remembrance of their Lord﴾, i.e., they do not even bring Him to mind, let alone fear His punishment, and they do not count the security and ease they enjoy as a protection and safeguarding, so that they might be asked about the one who guards: ﴿Or do they have gods who can defend them against Us? They are unable even to help themselves, nor will they be accompanied (protected) from Us.﴾ [al-Anbiya: 43], i.e., for these who hasten their Lord's punishment, are there gods who can prevent them, if We bring down Our punishment upon them and send Our might upon them, from Us? Its meaning: Do they have gods other than Us who can prevent them from Us? Then the Exalted, whose praise is great, described those gods with weakness and humiliation and with what they are in terms of their attributes. Its meaning: how can their gods, whom they invoke other than Us, prevent them from Us, when they cannot help themselves and are not accompanied by Us with help and support? Ibn Jarir conveyed this.

So ﴿fa-yusbahuna﴾ (﴿yuṣḥabūna﴾) here carries the meaning of "to be given protection" (yujarun). It is said: "May God accompany you" (ṣahibaka Allah), i.e., may He grant you protection and keep you safe, as in al-Asas (Asas al-Balagha). Ibn Jarir said: i.e., they will not be accompanied by protection, because the Arabs have a reported usage: "I am your protector (jar) from so-and-so and your companion (sahib)," meaning: "I grant you protection and defend you." If they are not accompanied by protection, there will be no one to prevent them from the punishment of God, given His wrath upon them, so they will not be accompanied with good and will not be helped.

The discussion of the words of His Exalted saying:

[44] ﴿Nay, We gave enjoyment to these people and their fathers until life stretched long upon them. Do they not see that We come upon the land, reducing it from its outlying parts? Are they then the victors?﴾

﴿Nay, We gave enjoyment to these people and their fathers until life stretched long upon them﴾ is a turning away (idrab) from what they had imagined, explaining that what drove them to their error and obstinacy is what they were given enjoyment of in the worldly life, and what they and those before them delighted in, until the term (al-amad) stretched long upon them. No warning from punishment, nor deterrent from retribution, came to them, until they reckoned that they were upon something and that they could not be overcome. ﴿Do they not see that We come upon the land, reducing it from its outlying parts?﴾ That is: We diminish the land of disbelief, ruining it from its sides by Our subduing its people, Our victory over them, their expulsion from it, and their slaughter by the sword, so that they might take heed from that, be admonished by it, and beware of Us lest We send down Our might upon them in the manner of what We sent down upon those among the people of the outlying regions who were treated thus. This is related from Ibn Jarir. And this is like His Exalted saying: ﴿And We destroyed what is around you of the towns, and We varied the signs, that they might return﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 27]. And His Exalted saying: ﴿Are they then the victors?﴾ (p-4276) That is: are these polytheists, who seek to hasten the punishment, the victors over Us, when they have seen Our subduing of those in whose courtyard We have made Our might descend, in the outlying parts of the earth?

In the definite article there is an allusion (ta'rid) that He, Exalted, is the Victor, known for subjugation.

The discussion concerning His saying, exalted is He:

[45] ﴿Say: I only warn you by revelation, but the deaf do not hear the call when they are warned.﴾

﴿Say: I only warn you by revelation﴾ That is: the revelation of God, which He sends down to me from Him, and with which I warn you of His punishment, not by bringing what you are hastening for, because that is not up to me, in keeping with the wisdom in this mission, which was built on rational proofs, not on sensory extraordinary feats, as we have previously mentioned. Then He pointed to the completeness of their ignorance and obstinacy, in that this warning does not benefit them, by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿but the deaf do not hear the call when they are warned﴾. That is: they do not attend with the hearing of their hearts to remembering what is in God's revelation of admonitions and reminders, so that they might be reminded by them, take heed, and be restrained when it is recited to them. Rather, they turn away from taking heed of it and reflecting upon it, like the act of the deaf person who does not hear what is said to him so that he may act upon it. As for restricting their deafness with His saying, ﴿when they are warned﴾, although they do not hear either warning or good tidings, this is either because the context is one of warning, or because one who does not hear when he is threatened, how would he hear in other circumstances? So it is more emphatic.

The interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[46] ﴿And if a breath of the punishment of your Lord should touch them, they would surely say, "Woe to us! Indeed, we were wrongdoers."﴾

﴿And if a breath of the punishment of your Lord should touch them, they would surely say, "Woe to us! Indeed, we were wrongdoers."﴾ That is: even if something of the least of His punishment, Exalted is He, were to reach them, they would submit, be humbled, and acknowledge that they had wronged themselves through their deafness, their turning away, their worship of those gods, and their abandonment of the worship of the One who created them.

(p-4277) A subtle point (laṭīfah):

In the opening of the verse there are several intensifications: the mention of touching (mass); what is conveyed by "nafḥah" of the meaning of smallness, for the origin of nafkh (blowing) is the wafting of the scent of a thing; the pattern (bināʾ) indicating the single occurrence; and the indefiniteness (tankīr). And His saying, Exalted is He:

**The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:**

[47] ﴿And We shall set up the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection, so no soul will be wronged in the least. Even if it is the weight of a mustard seed, We will bring it forth. And sufficient are We as reckoners.﴾

﴿And We shall set up the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection﴾ is an explanation of what will happen when that which they were warned of arrives. That is, We will establish the true, just scales by which the records of deeds are weighed. It has also been said that "setting up the scales" is a figurative expression for establishing a sound reckoning and a recompense according to deeds, with justice and equity, such that not even an atom's weight is wronged. The scales are described as *al-qist* (justice) in the singular form because it is a verbal noun (*masdar*) used as a descriptor for emphasis, as if they were themselves embodiments of justice. Or it is by omitting a noun, meaning "possessors of justice." It has also been said that it is an object of purpose (*mafʿul lahu*). The *lam* in *li-yawm al-qiyamah* is for causation, or means "in," that is, for the recompense of the Day of Resurrection, or for its people, or within it.

﴿so no soul will be wronged in the least﴾ means, in any of its rights. That is, not even a little of injustice. Rather, every possessor of a right will be paid his right in full. Even if the deed or the wrong is ﴿the weight of a mustard seed, We will bring it forth﴾, meaning We will bring forward that deed, which is expressed by the weight of a mustard seed, for weighing. The feminine form *utinna* is used because it is related to *habbah* (seed), which is feminine. And ﴿sufficient are We as reckoners﴾ means that whoever witnesses that station will be sufficed by Us as reckoners, because no one knows their deeds better than Us, and whatever good or evil they did in the world is known to Us.

The commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 21, verse 50:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[50] ﴿And this is a blessed reminder which We have sent down. Then will you deny it?﴾

﴿And this﴾, i.e., the noble Qur'an: ﴿a reminder﴾, i.e., one by which whoever is willing to be mindful is reminded: ﴿blessed﴾, i.e., abundant in good and benefit: ﴿which We have sent down. Then will you deny it?﴾, i.e., despite the evident fact that its descent is like the giving of the Torah. In the interrogative of denial there is a rebuke to them, that it is not fitting for them to deny it while they recognize the excellences of its inimitability. And the placing of (lahu, "to it") first is for the sake of the rhyme (fasila), or for the sake of restriction (hasr): because they acknowledge other things that are in the hands of the People of the Book.

The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[51] ﴿And We had certainly given Abraham his rectitude before, and We were of him well-Knowing.﴾

﴿And We had certainly given Abraham his rectitude﴾ means: his guidance to the truth, which is pure monotheism (tawhid). ﴿Before﴾ means: before Moses and Aaron. ﴿And We were of him well-Knowing﴾ means: We knew that he was worthy of what We had given him. Or: We knew that he combined the noble qualities of character which We had given him, so We qualified him for Our friendship (khullah) and purified him for Our choosing.

The Discourse on the Interpretation of His Words, exalted is He:

[52] "When he said to his father and his people, 'What are these images to which you are devoted?'"

"When he said to his father and his people, 'What are these images to which you are devoted?'" That is: what are these base figures to which you have devoted yourselves in worship? It is a question of contempt for them and a rebuke for devotion to their worship, [pointing out] that they are images and statues without spirit, fashioned objects that neither harm nor benefit, so how can they be worshipped?

The commentary on the saying of Allah, Exalted:

[53] ﴿They said, "We found our fathers worshipping them."﴾ [54] ﴿He said, "Indeed you and your fathers have been in clear error."﴾ [Al-Anbiya: 53–54]

﴿They said, "We found our fathers worshipping them."﴾ That is, we followed them in imitation (taqlid) and took them as our example (ta'assi).

﴿He said, "Indeed you and your fathers have been in clear error."﴾ [Al-Anbiya: 54] That is, it is not hidden from any person of reason that neither party rests on proof; rather, they rest on a followed desire and an obeyed devil. The use of (fi, "in") denoting containment indicates that they are firmly settled in their error, and that it is an ancient, inherited error. Thus it is more emphatic than (dallin, "astray").

(p-٤٢٨٠) The interpretation of His saying:

[55] ﴿They said: "Have you brought us the truth, or are you among the players?"﴾ [56] ﴿He said: "Rather, your Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, who originated them, and I am among the witnesses to that."﴾ [al-Anbiya: 55–56].

﴿They said: "Have you brought us the truth"﴾, i.e., in earnest, in the claim of prophethood and in attributing error to us: ﴿or are you among the players?﴾ ﴿He said: "Rather, your Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, who originated them, and I am among the witnesses to that."﴾ [al-Anbiya: 56]. Al-Zamakhshari (may God have mercy on him) said: The pronoun in (فَطَرَهُنَّ) refers either to the heavens and the earth, or to the statues (al-tamathil). Its referring to the statues is more effective in misleading them (tadlil) and more firmly established as an argument (ihtijaj) against them. That is, because it explicitly indicates that they are created and not fit for divinity (uluhiyya), unlike the first reading.

His answer, peace be upon him, is either a retraction (idrab) from the basis on which their statement was built, namely their belief that they are lords to them, as their saying clearly expresses: ﴿We worship idols, and we remain devoted to them﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 71]. It is as if it was said: "The matter is not so; rather, ﴿your Lord﴾ [al-Anbiya: 56], and so on." Or it is a retraction from his being a player, by establishing proof for what he claimed.

His saying ﴿among the witnesses﴾ [al-Anbiya: 56] means: those who attest to it with proof, not those who attest to your statement, which is devoid of it.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[57] ﴿And by Allah, I will surely scheme against your idols after you have turned away, retreating.﴾

﴿And by Allah, I will surely scheme against your idols﴾: I will certainly devise a plan to expose them by showing their helplessness. ﴿After you have turned away, retreating﴾: i.e., away from them, once you have finished worshipping them.

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[58] ﴿So he reduced them to fragments, except a large one among them, that they might return to it.﴾

(p-4281) ﴿So he reduced them to fragments﴾, i.e., broken pieces, after they had turned their backs on them, so that they would know that they cannot be rendered powerless to this extent. Thus he (Ibrahim) showed them their incapacity to defend themselves. Hence their worshipper's expectation that they would defend themselves is the utmost folly: ﴿except a large one among them, that they might return to it﴾, i.e., that they might ask it: "Why did you do this to our gods?" If its inability to speak has become evident, then whoever is beneath it is even more incapable in that respect, let alone able to repel the one who revealed their incapacity in this matter. So they returned and came to the house of the idols and found them reduced to fragments.

"The discussion concerning the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[59] ﴿They said, "Who has done this to our gods? Indeed, he is among the wrongdoers."﴾

﴿They said, "Who has done this?"﴾ That is, this monstrous deed. ﴿"To our gods. Or for his excess in smashing and breaking them, and his persistence in treating them with contempt. Or for exposing himself to destruction. The interrogative is for denunciation, reproach and vilification."

(p-4282)The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[62] ﴿They said: "Did you do this to our gods, O Ibrahim?"﴾ [63] ﴿He said: "Rather, it was done by this, their chief. So ask them, if they can speak."﴾ [al-Anbiya: 62–63].

﴿They said: "Did you do this to our gods, O Ibrahim?"﴾ ﴿He said: "Rather, it was done by this, their chief."﴾ [al-Anbiya: 63] Meaning: the one who left it did not break it. If you doubt that it was my act or its act, then ﴿ask them﴾ [al-Anbiya: 63], i.e., let them answer you, ﴿if they can speak﴾ [al-Anbiya: 63], i.e., the most evident is their total incapacity, which prevents attributing divinity to them. The position on this is that the intention of Ibrahim, may the blessings of Allah be upon him, was not to attribute the act issuing from him to the idol. Rather, he intended to establish it for himself and to affirm it for them through an allusive style by which he attained his aim of imposing the proof upon them and rebuking them. It may be said: those idols angered him when he saw them lined up in order. The anger of their chief was greater and more intense, because of what he saw of the increase in their veneration of him. So he attributed the act to him, because he is the one who was the cause of their being belittled and smashed, and an act is attributed both to its doer and to the one who motivated it. Thus it is an figurative speech by which he, peace be upon him, intended to alert them to the wrath of Allah, exalted is He, upon them for associating others with Him in worship by worshipping idols. It is related that he said: "This, their chief, did it," meaning that he was angry that these small ones were worshipped alongside him while he is greater than them. So it is as if it was said: "That great one did it according to your own doctrine, and the matter is possible." The most apparent of these aspects is the first. Imam Ibn Hazm relied upon it in his book (al-Fasl) in refuting those who permit sins upon the prophets, and his words are: "As for his saying, peace be upon him: ﴿Rather, it was done by this, their chief﴾ [al-Anbiya: 63], it is only a reproach and rebuke to them, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Taste it! Indeed, you are the mighty, the noble﴾ [al-Dukhan: 49], while in reality he is humiliated, abased, degraded, and tormented in the Fire. Both statements are a rebuke to those to whom they were addressed, according to their assumption that the idols do good and evil, and according to the assumption of the one being punished in this world that he is mighty and noble. Ibrahim did not say this (p-4283) as a confirmed statement because their chief did it, since lying is only reporting something contrary to what it is, with the intention of asserting that. And it is clear that his intention, peace be upon him, in any case, was only to direct them towards reflecting on the condition of their idols, as his saying indicates: ﴿So ask them, if they can speak﴾ [al-Anbiya: 63], i.e., if they are among those who can speak." Abu al-Su'ud said: "He, peace be upon him, did not say: 'if they can hear or understand,' even though questioning also depends on hearing and understanding, because the outcome of a question is the answer, and their not speaking is more evident, and rebuking them with that is more penetrating. This had already occurred first, as expressed by the saying of the Exalted:"

So it is as if it was said: "That great one did it according to your own doctrine, and the matter is possible." The most apparent of these aspects is the first. Imam Ibn Hazm relied upon it in his book (al-Fasl) in refuting those who permit sins upon the prophets, and his words are: "As for his saying, peace be upon him: ﴿Rather, it was done by this, their chief﴾ [al-Anbiya: 63], it is only a reproach and rebuke to them, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Taste it! Indeed, you are the mighty, the noble﴾ [al-Dukhan: 49], while in reality he is humiliated, abased, degraded, and tormented in the Fire. Both statements are a rebuke to those to whom they were addressed, according to their assumption that the idols do good and evil, and according to the assumption of the one being punished in this world that he is mighty and noble. Ibrahim did not say this (p-4283) as a confirmed statement because their chief did it, since lying is only reporting something contrary to what it is, with the intention of asserting that. And it is clear that his intention, peace be upon him, in any case, was only to direct them towards reflecting on the condition of their idols, as his saying indicates: ﴿So ask them, if they can speak﴾ [al-Anbiya: 63], i.e., if they are among those who can speak." Abu al-Su'ud said: "He, peace be upon him, did not say: 'if they can hear or understand,' even though questioning also depends on hearing and understanding, because the outcome of a question is the answer, and their not speaking is more evident, and rebuking them with that is more penetrating. This had already occurred first, as expressed by the saying of the Exalted:"

The discussion on the interpretation (ta'wil) of His saying, exalted is He:

[64] ﴿So they returned to themselves and said, "Indeed, it is you who are the wrongdoers."﴾

﴿So they returned to themselves﴾ means they consulted their intellects ('uqūl). Consulting the intellect is a metaphor for reflection and contemplation. By "the self" (nafs) is meant the rational soul (al-nafs al-nāṭiqah), and returning to it is an expression of what has been mentioned.

﴿Then they said, "Indeed, it is you who are the wrongdoers."﴾ That is, by this question, or by worshipping one that does not speak, does not harm, and does not benefit, rather than the one who broke them. So why do you attribute wrongdoing to him by your saying: ﴿Indeed, he is among the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Anbiya: 59].

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[65] ﴿Then they were turned back upon their heads: "You certainly know that these do not speak."﴾

﴿Then they were turned back upon their heads﴾ means: out of shame at their own deficiency, and in submission and yielding before Ibrahim, saying: ﴿You certainly know that these do not speak﴾, meaning: speech is not among their characteristics, so how can you order us to ask them?

(p-4284) The discussion on the interpretation (ta'wil) of His saying:

[66] ﴿He said, "Do you then worship, besides Allah, that which can neither benefit you at all nor harm you?"﴾ [67] ﴿"Uff to you and to what you worship besides Allah! Do you not then use your reason?"﴾ [al-Anbiya': 67]. Meaning: wretched is your conduct in worshipping what neither harms nor benefits.

Note (tanbih):

Al-Zamakhshari mentioned in *al-Kashshaf*, regarding His saying, ﴿Then they were turned back upon their heads﴾ [al-Anbiya': 65], four aspects. The summary of these, as in *al-'Inayah*, is that *al-tankis* (turning over) means reversing a thing by making its top its bottom. It may be used figuratively for returning from the upright thinking, in wronging themselves, to the corrupt thinking that permits worshipping them, despite their incapacity, let alone their being fit for divinity. So His saying, ﴿You certainly know﴾ [al-Anbiya': 65], means: it was not hidden from us and from you that they are thus, and that we have taken them as gods while knowing this. The evidence for this is His saying, ﴿Do you then worship﴾, and so on. Or, *al-tankis* means returning from false argument to the truth in their saying, ﴿You certainly know﴾, because it is a denial of their power and an acknowledgment that they are not fit for divinity. It was called *(naks)* [reversal] even though it was true, because it did not benefit them given their persistence, yet it is a reversal relative to what they were upon of falsehood. Or, *al-naks* is an intensification of their lowering of their heads in shame, and their saying, ﴿You certainly know﴾, was out of their bewilderment, and they brought forth what was a proof against them. Or, *al-naks* is an intensification of bewilderment and the cutting off of their argument.

﴿Uff﴾ [al-Anbiya': 67] is a sound which, when uttered, indicates that the one uttering it is vexed. There are many dialectal forms of it, as in the books of lexicography.

Al-Zamakhshari said: What vexed him (Abraham) was what he saw of their steadfastness in worshipping them after their excuse had been cut off, and after the truth had become clear and falsehood had vanished, so he expressed displeasure at them. When they were unable to argue, they turned to harming him, as is the way of the falsifier when his doubt is struck with proof: no one is more hateful to him than the one who is right, and he has no recourse left except to oppose him.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 21, verse 68:

(p-4285) The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[68] ﴿They said, "Burn him and support your gods, if you are to act."﴾

﴿They said, "Burn him"﴾, i.e., because he deserved the severest punishment in their view, and fire is the most terrifying thing with which one can be punished. ﴿And support your gods﴾, i.e., by avenging them. ﴿If you are to act﴾, i.e., to take some measure of retribution (siyasah) against him, for nothing else befits him.

The commentary on His saying, the Exalted:

[69] ﴿We said, "O fire, be coolness and safety upon Abraham."﴾

﴿We said﴾, meaning: to incapacitate them and their idols, to show care for the one We sent, and to confirm him in the deliverance of those who believed in him. ﴿O fire, be coolness﴾, meaning: be cool upon Abraham, although you burn firewood. ﴿And safety upon Abraham﴾, meaning: do not go so far in coldness as to destroy him, but be non-harmful. It was permitted that "safety" (salaman) be in the accusative, governed by a verb implied by its context. The command is a metaphor for subjugation, as in His saying: ﴿Be apes, despised﴾ [al-A'raf: 166]. In it there is an implicit metaphor (isti'arah bi'l-kinayah), by likening the fire to an obedient subordinate, and by imagining for it a command and a call. For this reason Abu Muslim said: the meaning is that He, glory be to Him and exalted, made the fire coolness and safety, not that there was any speech, as in His saying: ﴿Say to it "Be," and it is﴾ [Ya-Sin: 82], meaning: so it becomes. The fire is inanimate, and it is not permissible to address it. This is evident.

Note:

Al-Razi said: concerning the manner in which the fire became cool, there are three opinions:

The first: that God, exalted, removed from it the heat and burning, and left in it the light and brightness. And God is powerful over all things.

The second: that God, exalted, created in Abraham's body a condition that prevents the harm of the fire from reaching him, as He does with the guardians of Hell in the Hereafter, and as He constructed the body of the ostrich such that swallowing a heated iron does not harm it, and the body of the salamander (al-samandal) such that remaining in fire does not harm it.

The third: that He, glory be to Him, created between him and the fire a barrier that prevents the effect of the fire from reaching him.

The verifying scholars (al-muhaqqiqun) said: the first is preferable, because the apparent meaning of His saying ﴿O fire, be coolness﴾ is that the fire itself became cool, so that Abraham was spared its effect, not that the fire remained as it was.

The discussion concerning the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[70] ﴿And they intended a scheme against him, but We made them the greatest losers.﴾ [71] ﴿And We delivered him and Lot to the land which We had blessed for all the worlds.﴾ [al-Anbiya′: 71].

﴿And they intended a scheme against him, but We made them the greatest losers﴾ That is: they intended to plot against him by harming him, but they were none other than defeated and subdued. Al-Zamakhshari said: They overcame him with argument, but God overpowered him and gave him a rebuttal that silenced them. And they resorted to force and tyranny, but He gave him victory and strengthened him. ﴿And We delivered him and Lot﴾ [al-Anbiya′: 71], that is, because he had emigrated with him, ﴿to the land which We had blessed for all the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya′: 71], and it is the land of al-Sham. It was blessed by the multitude of prophets, by the sending down of the sacred laws which are the path to both happinesses, and by the abundance of blessings, fertility, fruits, and the good living of both the rich and the poor. Ibrahim, peace be upon him, settled in Filastin, and Lot, peace be upon him, in Sodom.

The commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 21, verse 72:

Then He explained His blessing upon Ibrahim by His saying:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[72] ﴿And We bestowed upon him Ishaq and Ya'qub as an additional gift, and We made them all righteous.﴾

﴿And We bestowed upon him Ishaq﴾, i.e., in answer to his supplication: ﴿My Lord, grant me [a child] from among the righteous﴾ [al-Saffat: 100]. ﴿And Ya'qub as an additional gift﴾, i.e., an increase and a bounty, without his having asked for it. Then He indicated that the source of the blessing in them both is righteousness, by His saying: ﴿and We made them all righteous﴾, through uprightness and being firmly established in guidance.

The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Saying, Exalted is He:

[73] ﴿And We made them leaders guiding by Our command, and We revealed to them the doing of good deeds, the establishment of prayer, and the giving of zakah; and they were worshippers of Us.﴾

﴿And We made them leaders﴾ meaning: exemplars who are followed in matters of religion, in answer to his supplication, peace be upon him, when he said: ﴿and [make leaders] from my offspring﴾ [Ibrahim: 40]. ﴿guiding by Our command﴾ meaning: guiding people to the truth by Our command to them to do so and Our permission. Al-Zamakhshari said: In this is [the indication] that whoever is fit to be an exemplar in the religion of Allah, guidance is incumbent upon him; he is commanded by Allah to undertake it, and it is not permissible for him to neglect it or be slack in it. The first part of this is that he be guided himself, because the benefit of his guidance is more general, and souls are more inclined to follow one who is guided. ﴿and We revealed to them the doing of good deeds﴾ meaning: that they should do good deeds, of what pertains to the hearts or the limbs; ﴿the establishment of prayer, and the giving of zakah; and they were worshippers of Us﴾ meaning: with pure monotheism and righteous action.

The discourse on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[74] ﴿And Lot—We gave him judgment and knowledge, and We saved him from the town that used to commit wicked deeds. Indeed, they were a people of evil, defiantly disobedient.﴾ [75] ﴿And We admitted him into Our mercy. Indeed, he was among the righteous.﴾ [al-Anbiya': 74–75].

﴿And Lot—We gave him judgment﴾: i.e., wisdom, which is what must be practiced. ﴿And knowledge﴾: i.e., that which the prophets ought to know. Allah sent him to Sodom, and its people denied him and opposed him, so Allah destroyed them and overturned upon them what He related in more than one place in His Mighty Book. He alluded to this within his statement, in explaining His care for him and His honoring of him: ﴿and We saved him from the town﴾, i.e., from its punishment: ﴿that used to commit wicked deeds﴾ (p-4288), meaning sodomy, which was the most abominable of their deeds, and by which they deserved destruction. For this reason some jurists held that the sodomite should be thrown down headfirst from a high place and stones should be cast upon him, as was done to them. ﴿Indeed, they were a people of evil, defiantly disobedient.﴾ ﴿And We admitted him into Our mercy﴾ [al-Anbiya': 75], i.e., into its people: ﴿Indeed, he was among the righteous﴾ [al-Anbiya': 75], i.e., those who act upon knowledge, steadfast in uprightness.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[76] ﴿And Noah, when he called out before; so We answered him and saved him and his family from the great distress.﴾

﴿And Noah, when he called out before⦆ means: he invoked his Lord for the destruction of his people when they denied him, saying: ﴿I am overpowered, so help [me]﴾ [al-Qamar: 10] ﴿My Lord, do not leave upon the earth from among the disbelievers an inhabitant﴾ [Nuh: 26]. ﴿So We answered him and saved him and his family from the great distress﴾, which is the flood, or [it may mean] from the hardship, the denial and the harm. For he remained among them a thousand years less fifty years, calling them to God, mighty and majestic, and only a few believed in Him.

The discourse on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[77] ﴿And We helped him against the people who denied Our signs. Indeed, they were a people of evil, so We drowned them all.﴾

﴿And We helped him against the people﴾, i.e., We gave him a victory that entailed triumph over and vengeance upon his people: ﴿who denied Our signs. Indeed, they were a people of evil, so We drowned them all﴾, i.e., not one of them remained, just as their Prophet had supplicated.

(p-٤٢٨٩) The discussion of the interpretation (ta'wil, meaning explanation) of His saying, exalted is He:

[78] ﴿And Dawud and Sulayman, when they were judging concerning the tilth, when the sheep of the people strayed into it at night, and We were witnesses to their judgment.﴾

﴿And Dawud and Sulayman, when they were judging concerning the tilth﴾ i.e., the crop (al-zar'). ﴿When the sheep of the people strayed into it﴾ i.e., grazed on it at night. ﴿And We were witnesses to their judgment﴾ i.e., to the judgment of the judges and of those who came to them for judgment, being knowing.

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He:

[79] ﴿So We gave understanding of it to Solomon. And to each We gave judgment and knowledge. And We subjected the mountains to exalt [Us] along with David, and the birds. And We were doing [it].﴾

﴿So We gave understanding of it﴾: that is, the verdict or the judgment, both understood from the context. ﴿to Solomon﴾: that is, his judgment in it was [accepted as] his judgment, not his father's judgment. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that sheep damaged a crop at night, so David ruled that the sheep [be given] to the owners of the field. Solomon said: "Rather, the sheep should be taken and handed over to the owners of the crop, so that they may have their offspring, their milk and their benefits. The owners of the sheep should sow for the people of the crop a crop like theirs, so that they may cultivate and restore it. When the crop reaches the state it was in on the night the sheep grazed in it, the owners of the field take it back and return the sheep to their owners." Similarly it is related from Ibn Masʿud, as a statement of his (mawqūf) and not as a prophetic report (marfūʿ). And God knows best the reality.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And to each We gave judgment and knowledge﴾: that is, to each of the two of them We gave wisdom and abundant knowledge, not to Solomon alone. In this there is a removal of what might be suggested by singling out Solomon, peace be upon him, for understanding, namely that David's judgment, peace be upon him, was not a legal judgment (ḥukm sharʿī).

(p. 4290) Remarks:

The first: The verse has been cited as evidence that the error of a mujtahid (one who exerts independent juristic reasoning, ijtihād) is forgiven. Some have reversed this and cited the verse as evidence that every mujtahid is correct (muṣīb).

He said: Because its outward meaning indicates that there is no ruling of God on this question prior to ijtihād, and that the truth is not one. The same applies to other cases, since there is no one who distinguishes between them; for if there were a ruling of God in it, it would be determined. This is the position of the Muʿtazila, as clarified in the principles of jurisprudence (uṣūl). It has been answered that the implication of His words ﴿So We gave understanding of it to Solomon﴾, in singling him out for understanding rather than David, peace be upon him, indicates that he was the one who hit the truth in the sight of God. Were it not so, singling him out for understanding would have no meaning. Those who cite the verse say: since God did not make him err, this shows that each of them was correct. Singling him out for understanding does not indicate David's error, peace be upon him, since it is possible that each was correct. But this [position] is more lenient, and that [position] is more fitting, in encouraging caution against harming others. For this reason everyone cites this verse. Just as God's ruling in it is not known, the determination of its implication is not known either. Thus [it is stated] in al-ʿInāya.

In Fatḥ al-Bayān there occurs, in substance: There is no doubt that it indicates the lifting of sin from the one who errs. As for each of them being correct, this verse does not indicate it, nor does any other; rather, the hadith agreed upon in the two Ṣaḥīḥs and elsewhere explicitly states that when a judge exerts ijtihād and hits the mark, he has two rewards, and if he exerts ijtihād and errs, he has one reward. So the Prophet ﷺ called him one who erred. How, then, can it be said that he is correct in accordance with God's ruling and in agreement with it? God's ruling, glorified is He, is one and does not vary with the variation of the mujtahids. Otherwise, it would follow that His ruling, Mighty and Majestic is He, depends on the ijtihādāt of the mujtahids, and the consequent is false, so the antecedent is likewise. Moreover, it would entail that the same thing about which the ijtihād of the mujtahids differs, as to permissibility and prohibition, would be both lawful and unlawful in God's ruling, glorified is He. This consequent is false by consensus, so the antecedent is likewise. Furthermore, it would follow that God's ruling, glorified is He, is continually renewed with the emergence of each mujtahid who has an ijtihād concerning that incident (p. 4291), and that what God, glorified and exalted is He, intends in it does not cease except with the cessation of the mujtahids. The consequent is false, so the antecedent is likewise. The conclusion is that mujtahids are unable to hit the truth in every incident, but they do not persist in error, just as David here returned to Solomon's ruling when it became clear to him that it was correct.

al-Ḥasan said: Were it not for this verse, I would have seen the judges as ruined, but God praised this one for his correctness and commended that one for his ijtihād.

The second: This verse indicates the permissibility of ijtihād for the prophets, peace be upon them. This is the position of the majority (jumhūr). Some have prohibited it, and they have no basis for this, because if David's judgment had been by revelation, the judgment of his son Solomon would not have been preferred over it. Among what clearly indicates its occurrence is His words, Exalted is He: ﴿God pardon you. Why did you give them permission?﴾ [al-Tawba: 43], so He reproached him for what had occurred from him. Had that been by revelation, He would not have reproached him. Among it is what is authentically transmitted from him, may the blessings of God be upon him, in his words: "Had I known at the beginning of my affair what I came to know at its end, I would not have brought the offering animals." Such a thing would not be in what he did by revelation. Similar instances are numerous in the Book and the Sunna. Also, istinbāṭ (deriving rulings by inference) is the highest rank of the scholars, so it must be that the Messenger had a part in it; otherwise each individual mujtahid would be superior to him in this domain.

al-Rāzī said: When it has become predominant in the opinion of a prophet that the ruling in the original case is caused (muʿallal) by a certain meaning, and then he knows or conjectures that this meaning exists in another case, he must conjecture that God's ruling in this case is like that in the original. He has a certain premise, namely that opposing God's ruling is a cause for deserving punishment. From these two premises arises a conjecture of deserving punishment for opposing this conjectured ruling. At this point, either he proceeds to act and to refrain simultaneously, which is impossible because of the impossibility of combining contradictories; or he refrains from both, which is impossible because of the impossibility of being free of contradictories; or he prefers the less probable over the more probable, which is false by the self-evident judgment of reason; or he prefers the more probable over the less probable, and that is acting by analogy (qiyās). This point is the one upon which reliance is placed for acting by analogy. And it also holds with respect to the prophets, peace be upon them. End.

The third: al-Suyūṭī said in al-Iklīl: It has been cited as evidence for the permissibility of ijtihād in the rulings and for its occurrence among the prophets. We have mentioned this before. It also shows that the mujtahid may err, and that he is rewarded despite the error and is not sinful, because He, Exalted is He, informed that the attainment of the truth was with Solomon, then He praised both of them. This has been mentioned earlier. It has also been cited by those who say that a judge, after his judgment based on ijtihād, returns to what is more probable than it. In it there is also the obligation on the owners of livestock to compensate for what their animals damage at night, not during the day, because trespass (nafsh) occurs only at night, as Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Shurayḥ, al-Zuhrī and Qatāda. Whoever generalizes the liability interprets it as grazing in general. A group, including al-Ḥasan, held that the owner of the crop is given the livestock, to benefit from their milk and wool until the crop returns to what it was, as Solomon ruled in this incident, since no abrogating text (nāsikh) definitively established in our law is known to them. End.

The fourth: Ibn Jarīr transmitted from ʿĀmir, who said: Two men came to Shurayḥ. One of them said: "The sheep of this man cut up some yarn of mine." Shurayḥ said: "By day or by night? If it was by day, the owner of the sheep is free of liability. If it was by night, he is liable." Then he recited this verse.

Ibn Kathīr said: What Shurayḥ said resembles what Imam Aḥmad, Abū Dāwūd and Ibn Māja transmitted through the chain of al-Layth ibn Saʿd, from al-Zuhrī, from Ḥarām ibn Muḥayyiṣa: "The camel of al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib (p. 4293) entered an orchard and damaged it. So the Messenger of God ﷺ ruled that the owners of the orchards are responsible for guarding them by day, and that what livestock damage by night is the liability of their owners." This hadith has been criticized for a defect (muʿallal). Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted that Iyās ibn Muʿāwiya, when he was appointed as a judge, was visited by al-Ḥasan, who wept. He said: "What makes you weep?" He said: "O Abū Saʿīd, it has reached me that of the judges: a man who exerted ijtihād and erred is in the Fire; a man whose desire inclined him is in the Fire; and a man who exerted ijtihād and hit the mark is in Paradise." Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said: "Among what God has related of the story of David and Solomon, peace be upon them, and the prophets, is a ruling that refutes the statement of these people." God said: ﴿And David and Solomon, when they judged concerning the field﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 78] to the end of the verse. So God praised Solomon, and did not blame David.

Then he said, meaning al-Ḥasan: God has imposed three things on the wise: that they not sell it for a small price; that they not follow desire in it; and that they not fear anyone in it. Then he recited: ﴿O David, indeed We have made you a vicegerent upon the earth, so judge between the people in truth and do not follow desire, lest it lead you astray from the way of God﴾ [Ṣād: 26], and He said: ﴿So do not fear the people, but fear Me﴾ [al-Māʾida: 44], and He said: ﴿And do not exchange My verses for a small price﴾ [al-Māʾida: 44].

Then Ibn Kathīr said: It is established in the Ṣaḥīḥ of al-Bukhārī from ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ that he said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "When the judge exerts ijtihād and hits the mark, he has two rewards; and when he exerts ijtihād and errs, he has one reward." This hadith explicitly refutes what Iyās imagined, namely that a judge who exerts ijtihād and errs is in the Fire.

In the Sunan: "Judges are of three kinds: one judge is in Paradise and two judges are in the Fire. A man who knew the truth (p. 4294) and judged by it is in Paradise. A man who judged between people in ignorance is in the Fire, and a man who knew the truth and judged contrary to it is in the Fire."

Then He, glorified is He, explained the particular honours of each of David and Solomon, after explaining the general honour for both of them, by His words: ﴿And We subjected the mountains to exalt [Us] along with David, and the birds. And We were doing [it].﴾ That is: We subjected the mountains and the birds to sanctify God along with him, with a voice that is manifested to him or created in them. Ibn Kathīr said: That was because of the beauty of his voice in reciting His Book, the Psalms (al-Zabūr). When he chanted it, the birds would stop in the air and respond to him, and the mountains would echo back to him in harmony. For this reason, when the Prophet ﷺ passed by Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī while he was reciting the Qur'an at night, and he had a very beautiful voice, he stopped and listened to his recitation and said: "He has been given a flute from the flutes of the family of David." He said: "O Messenger of God! Had I known that you were listening, I would have embellished it for you with embellishment."

Abū ʿUthmān al-Hindī said: I have never heard the sound of a cymbal, nor a lute, nor a flute like the voice of Abū Mūsā, may God be pleased with him. End.

The mention of the mountains before the birds is because their glorification is more wondrous and more indicative of power, and more effective in showing inimitability, since they are inanimate. The concluding phrase, ﴿And We were doing [it]﴾, indicates that it is not strange on the side of divine power, even if it is wondrous to those addressed. This verse is like His words, Exalted is He, in Sūrat Ṣād: ﴿And remember Our servant David, possessor of strength; indeed he was repentant﴾ [Ṣād: 17]. ﴿Indeed, We subjected the mountains to exalt [Us] with him at evening and sunrise﴾ [Ṣād: 18]. ﴿And the birds, gathered; all were to him returning [in devotion]﴾ [Ṣād: 19].

(p-4295) The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[80] ﴿And We taught him the making of coats of mail for you, to protect you from your violence. So will you not be grateful?﴾

﴿And We taught him the making of coats of mail for you﴾ — i.e., the work of making the armor (durū') to be worn. It has been said: the armor before him was plates, and he made them into rings (ḥalaqan) and interlaced them (sarada), i.e., made them into rings and inserted some into others, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We made iron soft for him﴾ [Saba': 10] ﴿Make full coats of mail and measure well the links﴾ [Saba': 11], i.e., do not make the ring too wide so that the nail becomes loose, and do not make the nail too thick so that the ring breaks. Therefore He said: ﴿to protect you from your violence﴾, i.e., to guard you from the wounds of your fighting. ﴿So will you not be grateful?﴾ — i.e., for the blessings of Allah upon you, for what He inspired His servant Dawud with, and taught him this as a mercy to you, by which your lives are preserved for you in the thick of battle. In presenting the command to give thanks in the form of a question, there is exaggeration in rebuke and reproach, because of what it implies of shortcoming in giving thanks.

The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[81] ﴿And to Solomon [We subjected] the wind, blowing forcefully, running by his command to the land which We had blessed. And We are ever Knowing of all things.﴾

﴿And to Solomon [We subjected] the wind, blowing forcefully﴾ — that is, We made it subservient to him. ﴿Running by his command to the land which We had blessed﴾ — which is Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). ﴿And We are ever Knowing of all things﴾ — that is, of what the perfect wisdom requires in this matter. This is like His words, Exalted is He: ﴿So We subjected to him the wind, running gently by his command wherever he directed﴾ [Sad: 36].

Al-Zamakhshari, may Allah have mercy on him, said: If you ask, "This wind is described as forceful at one time and gentle at another; how do these reconcile?" I say: In itself it was gentle and pleasant, like a breeze. When it passed beneath his throne, it carried him away in a short period of time, as He said: ﴿Its morning course was a month's journey and its evening course a month's journey﴾ [Saba: 12]. So its gathering of the two matters was that it was gentle in itself and forceful in its action, along with its obedience to Solomon and its blowing in accordance with what he wished and decreed, a sign leading to a sign and a miracle leading to a miracle.

In (al-Intisaf) he said: This is like what is reported in the description of Moses' staff, sometimes as a jann (a small, agile snake) and sometimes as a thu'ban (a large, thick snake). The jann is the slender of snakes and the thu'ban is the great, thick one among them. The reason for this is that it combined both descriptions: in its lightness and the speed of its movement it was like a jann, and in the greatness of its form it was like a thu'ban. Thus, according to this explanation, each of the wind and the staff contains two miracles. And Allah knows best.

[82] ﴿And of the devils were those who dove for him and did work other than that; and We were for them guardians.﴾

(p-4297) The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[83] ﴿And Job, when he called to his Lord, "Indeed, adversity has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful."﴾ [84] ﴿So We responded to him and removed what afflicted him of adversity. And We gave him his family and the like thereof with them as mercy from Us and a reminder for the worshippers.﴾ [al-Anbiya: 84]

﴿And Job, when he called to his Lord, "Indeed, adversity has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful."﴾ ﴿So We responded to him and removed what afflicted him of adversity. And We gave him his family and the like thereof with them as mercy from Us and a reminder for the worshippers.﴾ [al-Anbiya: 84] That is: remember Job, the trial that befell him, his supplication to his Lord for the removal of what had descended upon him, and God's response to his supplication, and the favour He bestowed upon him in lifting the trial. And [remember] what He multiplied for him after his patience of blessings, so that you may know that victory comes with patience, and that the outcome of hardship is ease. And that for you there is the example of such a patient prophet, in what sometimes befalls you of harm. And that the trial did not spare the prophets; rather they are the most tried of people, as in the hadith: "The most severely tried of people are the prophets, then the righteous, then the next best and the next best."

Among the causes of relief is his supplication to God, the earnest entreaty to Him and the humble pleading before Him, and mentioning Him by His most beautiful names and His exalted attributes. Trial does not indicate humiliation and wretchedness, for happiness and wretchedness in this world are not contingent upon good and bad deeds, because this world is not the abode of recompense. The fruit of truthfulness in patience is the full payment of reward and the multiplication of goodness. It has been narrated that Job, peace be upon him, when he was tested by the loss of his livelihood and the destruction of all his household, and by remaining for a time suffering pains from sores on his body, and he was patient and grateful, his Lord had mercy on him: the health of his body returned to him and he was given many times what he had lost. He was granted a number of children and lived a long life, seeing his children to the fourth generation. Therefore God, exalted is He, said: ﴿and a reminder for the worshippers﴾ [al-Anbiya: 84], meaning: a reminder for others among the worshippers (p-4298) so that they may be patient as he was patient, until they are rewarded as he was rewarded in this world and the Hereafter. In sum, the secret is the strengthening of the hearts of the believers and encouraging them to patience in striving in the path of truth. The exegetes have related here, concerning Job's trial, various narrations with weak chains, which the scholars of transmitted reports do not give any weight, nor do they give them the slightest consideration from the reliable. Yes, there exists in the Torah a book of Job containing a description of his harm, the loss of all his possessions, livestock and household, and the descent upon him of a severe illness, through which he lost rest and the pleasure of life, and which contains strange matters. However, not all of them are considered reliable, because of the admixture that entered them and the expansion into the extraneous, until the true and the false became mixed. And if a grave trial and a astonishing harm can be derived from their totality, [yet] had God known more good in them than what He summarized in His wise revelation, He would have graciously detailed it for us. Therefore one stops at His summary in what He summarized, and His detail in what He detailed.

Note:

Some have said: The majority of verifiers hold that Job lived after the time of Abraham, peace be upon them both. He was wealthy, one of the owners of estates and livestock, and a chief among his people. His possessions and dwelling were in a fertile land of excellent soil and abundant pasture, to the south-east of the Dead Sea, and from Mount Seir between the lands of Edom and the Arabian desert. And God knows best.

**The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:**

[87] ﴿And Dhu al-Nun, when he went off in anger, and thought that We would not decree (any hardship) for him, then he called out in the darkness, "There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I have been among the wrongdoers."﴾ [88] ﴿So We answered him and saved him from distress, and thus do We save the believers.﴾ [al-Anbiya: 88].

﴿And Dhu al-Nun, when he went off in anger, and thought that We would not decree (any hardship) for him, then he called out in the darkness, "There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I have been among the wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿So We answered him and saved him from distress, and thus do We save the believers.﴾ [al-Anbiya: 88] That is: remember Dhu al-Nun, meaning the companion of the fish, who is Yunus (peace be upon him), and his patience in what befell him, then his turning back (to God) and his deliverance, so that your heart may be firmly settled regarding his account, and your inner self may be strengthened to endure what the tyrants say. This story is mentioned here, in Surat al-Saffat, and in Surat al-Qalam. The reason is that Yunus ibn Matta (peace be upon him) was commanded by God to go to the people of Nineveh, from the land of Mosul, the seat of the rule of the Assyrians, to call them to faith in Him alone, to the establishment of justice, the spreading of equity, and good conduct. But they were the opposite of this: their disbelief had grown great and their evil had multiplied. He feared that the matter would not be accomplished for him among them, so he fled from Bayt al-Maqdis to Jaffa, and boarded a ship sailing to Tarshish to settle there. God sent a violent wind upon the sea, and the ship was nearly sinking with him aboard. The passengers lightened it of their goods, but this did not help. It came into their minds that there was a person in the ship on account of whom they would perish, so they cast lots to see who it was, and the lot fell upon Yunus. They threw him into the sea, and its turbulence and its waves subsided. God prepared a fish for Yunus, which swallowed him, and he remained in the belly of the fish for three days. Then he called upon his Lord, and He answered him, and the fish cast him onto the shore. Then God revealed to Yunus a second time that he should set out for Nineveh and call its people to God, Exalted is He. He reached it and proclaimed to them the Oneness (of God) and repentance. He warned them that if they did not believe, Nineveh would be overturned with them. When they became certain of this, they believed. So God lifted the punishment from them. God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Why was there not a town that believed so that its faith would benefit it, except the people of Yunus? When they believed, We removed from them the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world, and We let them enjoy (their lives) for a time.﴾ [Yunus: 98]

**Notes:**

**First:** Yunus (peace be upon him) is called Yunan in the Torah, and he is Hebrew. It is said that he was from Gath-hepher, a town in the tribe of Zebulun, in the north of the Holy Land. It is also said that he was sent as a prophet about eight hundred years before the Messiah. And God knows best.

**Second:** Most of the exegetes (as al-Razi related) hold that Yunus went off angry at his Lord. They hold that by fleeing to the ship, and by abandoning his journey to Nineveh at first, he thought that he would be left alone and would not be held to account. Some of the scholars of verification said: Yunus only opposed the divine command at first and took a concession regarding it, fearing that he would be thought a false prophet if the people of Nineveh repented and God pardoned their sin. The use of the intensive form in (mughadiban) is for emphasis, because its root implies a relation between two parties, each of whom strives hard to overcome the other. It therefore requires exerting one's utmost power and reaching the extreme, so it is used for its consequence, the intensification, without the sense of (mufa'ala) (reciprocal action) being intended. The apparent meaning of this verse and similar verses has been used as evidence by those who hold that prophets may commit error, except lying in conveying the message, for error in it is not permissible for them, since it is the proof of God over His servants; and except in what pertains to the explanation of revelation, for error is not permissible for them when explaining what is legislated. This is the view of the Karramiyya (a sect) against the Murji'a, as in the commentary on Nahj al-Balagha by Ibn Abi al-Hadid. (The view of al-Baqillani of the Ash'ariyya (as related by Ibn Hazm in al-Milal)): As for the majority who prevent that, they have interpretations for this verse and its like. We prefer what Ibn Hazm said on this matter, because he was more outspoken. He, may God have mercy on him, said, after relating the view of the Karramiyya mentioned above: The Ahl al-Sunna, the Mu'tazila, the Najjariyya, the Kharijites, and the Shi'a hold that it is absolutely impossible for a prophet to commit deliberate disobedience, whether a minor or a major sin.

He then said: This is the view by which we religiously submit to God, Exalted is He, and it is not permissible for anyone to hold any other. We say: Forgetfulness without intent may occur from prophets. They may also intend something seeking the face of God, Exalted is He, and nearness to Him by it, and it may then coincide with what is contrary to God's intended purpose. However, God, Exalted is He, never confirms them in either of these two aspects at all, but rather He will certainly alert them to this after it occurs from them. Sometimes He makes them dislike what is undesirable in this world, as happened to Adam, Yunus, and the (other) prophets (peace be upon them), unlike us in this regard. For we are not held to account for what we forget, nor for what we intend by seeking the face of God, Mighty and Majestic, when it does not coincide with His intended purpose. Rather, we are rewarded for this with one reward.

He then said (in discussing Yunus, peace be upon him): As for God's report that Yunus went off angry, he never became angry at his Lord, nor did God say that he was angry with his Lord. Whoever adds this addition has attributed a lie to God and added to the Qur'an what is not in it. This is not permissible, and it is not allowable to suspect of anyone with even a little measure of intellect that he would be angry with his Lord, Exalted is He. How then could a prophet from among the prophets do such a thing? We therefore know with certainty that he was only angry with his people, and this did not coincide with the intended purpose of God, Mighty and Majestic, so he was punished for it, even though Yunus (peace be upon him) only intended by it the pleasure of God, Mighty and Majestic. As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and thought that We would not decree (any hardship) for him﴾, it is not as they imagined, a feeble opinion that is not permissible to attribute even to a weak woman or a weak man, unless one has reached the utmost ignorance. How then could it be attributed to a prophet who is preferred over people in knowledge? It is an absolutely certain impossibility that a prophet should think that God, Exalted is He, who sent him with His religion, is unable to do something, while he sees that a human like himself is able to do it. There is no doubt that whoever attributes this to the Prophet ﷺ, the virtuous one, his anger would intensify if it were attributed to him or to his son. How much more so to Yunus ibn Matta, about whom the Messenger of God ﷺ said: ««Do not prefer me over Yunus ibn Matta»». Thus their assumption is without doubt invalid, and it is established that the meaning of His saying: ﴿and thought that We would not decree (any hardship) for him﴾ is: We would not constrict for him, as He said, Exalted is He: ﴿As for when He tests him and restricts his provision﴾ [al-Fajr: 16], that is, constricted for him. Yunus (peace be upon him) thought that God, Exalted is He, would not constrict for him in his anger at his people, since he thought he was doing good by that act. God, Mighty and Majestic, only forbade Muhammad ﷺ from being like the companion of the fish. Yes, God, Mighty and Majestic, forbade him from being angry at his people and commanded him to be patient with their harm and to be lenient with them. As for His saying, Exalted is He, that he deserved blame and reproach, and that had it not been for the blessing with which He overtook him, he would have remained punished in the belly of the fish, this is exactly what we have said, that prophets (peace be upon them) are held to account in this world for what they did, which they thought was good and a means of drawing near to God, Mighty and Majestic, when it did not coincide with the intended purpose of their Lord. In this sense, he acknowledged against himself that he had been among the wrongdoers. Wrongdoing is placing a thing in other than its proper place. When the Prophet (peace be upon him) placed anger in other than its proper place, he acknowledged wrongdoing in that. Not because he intended it while knowing that he had wronged. The words of Ibn Hazm end here.

I say: What opens the door to problems is delving deeply into the words, overdoing their explanation, generating meanings and implications for them, and expanding on their aspects to such an extent that it deadens the brilliance of the composition and the purity of its eloquence. It is well known that the Noble Revelation surpassed all other known styles of speech in its wondrous style. For this reason it is a verse that seizes the hearts with tenderness, harmony, eloquence, and order. You do not find in its words anything but the choicest for their delicacy, nor in its sentences anything but the most majestic in structure, nor in its allusions anything but the strongest in symbolism, nor in its metaphors anything but the highest in meaning. Among this is its practice in blame and warning, of casting speech in the most forceful and emphatic mold, from which the severity of the matter and the strength of the reproach are understood. This is because of the might of the divine presence and the lordly station. Thus the eloquent Arab by nature, who has an innate taste, when the summary account of Yunus (peace be upon him) is recited to him in this verse, is astonished by what it conveys of the strength of reproach and blame, and that by fleeing he angered his master with an anger not comparable to the anger at the disobedient. For the good deeds of the righteous are the sins of those brought near (to God). He thought he would be forgotten and not held to account, and would escape and not be confined, but there came to him what had not been in his mind, and he fell into the snare of the power of the Most High. Then grace overtook him, and mercy reached him. This is the summary of what is understood from the verse, explicitly and implicitly. So understand what I have mentioned to you, for it will bring you as much verification as you hope for.

**Third:** Some atheists considered the swallowing of Yunus by the fish to be impossible. One of the scholars of verification replied that this is a denial of the power of God, the Originator of the heavens and the earth, who has marvels in His creation. Among them are the varied fish of enormous bodies, from which people still catch today, and in whose bellies are human bodies with their clothes. Another writer said: He did not specify the type of fish that swallowed Yunus.
